title: Call him Chief, Coach or Poppy, he answers to all of them | Bill Moor - NewsBreak
text:
By Bill Moor ,
1 days ago
THE NINE
A coin flip, a hiring freeze and a name change are three of the nine things that tell the story of South Bend Fire Chief Carl Buchanon:
1 The first 42 years of Carl’s life, he was Carl Hamilton. After a brief union with Carl's father, Howard Buchanon Sr., his mother Lee Anna took back her family name of Hamilton for both her and her young son.
“But I always wanted to change it to Buchanon,” Carl admits. “I didn’t feel that Hamilton was my real name. I felt cheated.”
The trouble was that he had made a name for himself as Carl Hamilton — as a firefighter … as a local high school track coach … and as a conference champ for Western Michigan University in the high hurdles. He also had three kids and his wife, Josie, who had gotten used to being Hamiltons.
But the whole family — with daughter LaToya already in college — gave the name change a thumbs up. So after all the paperwork and 42 years of waiting, Carl Buchanon he became.
2 Carl and his older brother, Howard Buchanon Jr., didn’t grow up in the same household but they certainly knew each other. Yet when Carl applied for the fire department, he didn’t let Howard know. Howard, nine years older, was already a highly-respected firefighter who would later serve as fire chief before Carl.
“I wanted to make sure people knew that I earned it myself,” Carl says. “Howard was surprised when I told him I had applied.”
Later on when they were both on the department, nothing pleased Carl more then to hear Howard say, “That’s my little brother.”
3 Carl really hadn’t planned on being a firefighter. But after a few years as a convenience store manager after college, he found himself bored. So when he saw the South Bend Fire Department was looking for recruits, he decided he might as well apply.
“When I got to the IUSB auditorium (for the introductory session), there were 500 to 600 people inside,” he remembers. “I asked an assistant chief at the door how many were going to be hired. He said three or four.” Carl was flabbergasted. “‘Well,’ he said to me, ‘You’re just going to have to be better than 596.’”
And he was — thanks in large part to his physical fitness.
“Then right before I was to be sworn in, I got a call from the city that there was a hiring freeze. I told them I already had quit my job. They said sorry.”
For a couple of years, he coached and did some part-time jobs until Fire Chief Luther Taylor called him and said the freeze was over. He wanted Carl on the department. Carl had some second thoughts after the long wait. So he talked to his mom and his pastor and then decided he wanted to serve the people and community.
“I thought I might try it for a couple of years.”
He is now in his 40th year — and has loved almost every minute of it.
Moor: Part of Irish wrestling royalty, still coaching Kingsmen at 85 | The 9
4 Carl was the fastest kid in his neighborhood and then the South Bend elementary school champ. One of his older friends was Greg Robertson, a state champion hurdler for LaSalle High School. ”Because of him, I wanted to be a hurdler, too.”
Unfortunately, Carl hit a hurdle so hard in practice that he broke it in half — and broke his foot, too. That happened his sophomore year before any meets had taken place. Yet by his junior season at Adams, he was good enough to place fourth in the state’s 120-yard high hurdles.
5 Then there was Carl’s senior season. He was undefeated going into the state meet and a co-favorite to win the highs. Mark Cammack of Fort Wayne Wayne was the other favorite. They were two lanes apart in the finals.
After the gun, the guy in between them hit the first hurdle and his hand made contact with Carl’s arm. It threw Carl off-stride. He fell behind Cammack but put on a furious effort to cause a photo finish.
Nobody knew who won, “but I thought I might have edged him,“ Carl says. “They took forever to announce the results, though. Events after ours were already being announced.”
The suspense kept building. “And then finally, they asked the coaches from South Bend Adams and Fort Wayne Wayne to report" to the officials’ tent.”
A little bit later. Adams coach Andy Mihail came back to where Carl was sitting. “‘I’m sorry Hambone — his nickname for me — I lost the toss,’” he said.
And, believe it or not, that’s how Carl was named the runner-up instead of the state champion — by a stupid coin toss.
Moor: Bethel music professor grew up tough during Vietnam War | The 9
6 But Carl has been able to savor state championships. For 20-plus years, his battalion chiefs allowed him to arrange his schedule so he could coach track at Adams and then Clay, He was able to coach his three kids, and daughter LaToya anchored Clay’s 400-meter relay to a state title in 2000. Her brothers, Carl II and Jarrod, were second and third, respectively, in the state hurdles.
LaToya married Adrian Swanson, who had won the state in the 300-meter hurdles for Adams in 1997. And their daughter Adriana — Carl’s granddaughter — captured the 100 high hurdles in the state finals last year as a Washington High junior. She will go for a repeat this season.
You could very well call this family the House of Hurdles.
7 There have been other kinds of hurdles in Carl’s life. He lost his first wife, Josie, 12 years ago after she battled MS for several years. They met while they both competed at Western Michigan. They later coached together.
He also has battled prostate cancer — diagnosed three years ago. He now serves as an advocate for early check-ups and for younger men to be vigilant about their health.
8 Carl misses hearing the alarms go off — the “tones” he calls them — and jumping on the truck. “Oh, would that adrenalin hit you,” he says. “You would get that tunnel vision coming out of the station and immediately start looking in the direction of the fire to see what kind of smoke it was.
“But I realize I‘m not 20-something anymore and I understand the importance of someone standing back and seeing the big picture.”
That’s his job now as chief, a job he has held for six years with a plan to keep doing it until he retires in 2028.
9 Three of Carl’s granddaughters (one from his second wife, Cathy’s side) call him Poppy, but 11-year-old Lilyana calls him Chief. Of course, his former track athletes still call him Coach.
He’ll gladly answer to any of them. All of those titles have to do with helping others. “And because of that, I feel so fortunate, so blessed.”
Bill Moor is a former sports editor and human interest columnist whose career started at The Tribune in 1973. Contact him at bry14zzo@gmail.com
